title: Short Stuff: All About Porcelain
summary: Short Stuff episode on porcelain, the last episode of 2025. Hosts describe porcelain as a dense, non-porous, durable ceramic made from clay, quartz and feldspar, fired at high temperatures (up to about 2300 F / 1260 C). They cover kaolin as the common porcelain clay, hard paste versus soft paste porcelain, translucency, and the origins in China during the Tang dynasty with refined forms developed in the Yuan dynasty, which Marco Polo brought back to Europe. They discuss how Europeans called it "china", the German alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger who cracked the European formula, Cornwall kaolin found in the 1770s, glazing being decorative rather than waterproofing, and vitrification. They touch on bisque (unglazed porcelain), porcelain tile cutting and forming, properties that make it prized (cleanability, water and bacteria resistance, recyclability), the record-priced Chinese Ming chicken cup sold for $36 million, and bone china made with bone ash. The episode ends with a year-end goodbye and thanks to the production team.

segments.title: Opening and year-end welcome
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the last Short Stuff episode of 2025 and announce that they will talk about porcelain.

segments.title: What porcelain is and its ingredients
segments.summary: Porcelain is described as a dense, durable, non-porous ceramic fired longer and hotter than ordinary clay. Its main ingredients are clay, quartz and feldspar, and the firing temperature and raw materials determine the type. Kaolin is named as the most common porcelain clay.

segments.title: Translucency and origins in China
segments.summary: Some porcelain is translucent. The hosts trace porcelain to Tang dynasty China, with refined forms developed in the Yuan dynasty and brought to Europe by Marco Polo.

segments.title: European demand, china name, and Böttger's discovery
segments.summary: Europeans prized imported Chinese porcelain but could not replicate it, which is why tableware is called china. German alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger reverse-engineered the process in the eighteenth century, and Cornwall kaolin was found in the 1770s. Hard paste and soft paste are introduced as the two main categories.

segments.title: Glazing and vitrification
segments.summary: The hosts note that glaze is decorative and does not make porcelain waterproof. Porcelain becomes impermeable because its materials vitrify during firing, becoming glassy.

segments.title: Bisque porcelain and seafood wordplay
segments.summary: Unglazed porcelain is called bisque. The hosts digress into a bit about pronouncing the word and comparing it to lobster bisque and langostino.

segments.title: Cutting and forming porcelain tile
segments.summary: Porcelain tile is durable for floors and walls but needs a wet tile saw because the blade gets hot. Smaller tiles up to about four by four feet are formed in molds; larger ones are made by pressing layers of ceramic powder.

segments.title: Why porcelain is prized and its value
segments.summary: Porcelain is valued for being natural, easy to clean, resistant to bacteria, water resistant, and recyclable through specialized recyclers. The Ming-era chicken cup sold at auction for about $36 million in 2014, which the hosts attribute to its rarity.

segments.title: Bone china
segments.summary: Bone china, developed by the English, uses bone ash, which the hosts say comes from farm animals rather than humans. It can be fired at lower temperatures but is less strong. The hosts make a joke about human bones.

segments.title: Year-end goodbye and thanks
segments.summary: The hosts say goodbye for the year and thank listeners, the producers and the writers.
